title: Barriers 2025 — Part C
source: WSU Y5 Barriers 2025 MCQ, student reconstruction; stems rewritten, tested point preserved

questions.stem: A patient with stable angina on metoprolol is started on a new antihypertensive. A subsequent ECG shows sinus bradycardia at 42/min.
questions.lead: Which drug was most likely prescribed?
questions.explanation: Verapamil (or diltiazem) plus a beta blocker is the classic combination that produces bradycardia and heart block. Dihydropyridines (nifedipine, amlodipine) do not slow the node.
questions.point: Non-dihydropyridine calcium blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) plus a beta blocker cause bradycardia and heart block; dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine) do not.

questions.stem: A patient collapses in a shopping centre. After 2 minutes of CPR the rhythm check shows ventricular tachycardia and a shock is delivered.
questions.lead: What is the next step?
questions.explanation: After any shock, immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes before the next rhythm check — no pulse check, no stacked shocks. Adrenaline comes after the 2nd shock (ANZCOR), amiodarone after the 3rd.
questions.point: After every defibrillation shock, resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes before rechecking rhythm — drugs come later (adrenaline after 2nd shock, amiodarone after 3rd per ANZCOR).

questions.stem: A well patient attends hospital insisting on 'the best doctor'. He is theatrical and dramatic in speech with shallow, rapidly shifting emotion, is flirtatious with nursing staff, and apologises for his appearance despite being well dressed.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Attention-seeking theatricality, exaggerated emotion and seductive/inappropriate interpersonal style is histrionic. Hypomania needs elevated mood, reduced sleep and increased activity; borderline is instability and fear of abandonment.
questions.point: Histrionic personality = attention-seeking, dramatic, shallow emotion, provocative interpersonal style; distinguished from hypomania by the absence of mood elevation and reduced sleep.

questions.stem: A patient with acute stroke has right hemiparesis and right-sided sensory loss.
questions.lead: What visual field defect would you expect?
questions.explanation: Right-sided motor and sensory loss is a left hemisphere lesion; the left optic radiation carries the right visual field, so the defect is a right homonymous hemianopia — same side as the weakness.
questions.point: A hemispheric stroke gives a homonymous hemianopia on the same side as the hemiparesis (left hemisphere → right hemianopia); bitemporal is chiasmal, monocular is pre-chiasmal.

questions.stem: A man strikes his head on a pavement. Forty minutes later he develops headache and falling consciousness.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Trauma, a lucid interval, then rapid deterioration is the extradural (middle meningeal artery) pattern — a lens-shaped bleed on CT. Subdurals are venous, slower, and typical in the elderly and anticoagulated.
questions.point: Head injury → lucid interval → rapid deterioration = extradural haematoma (middle meningeal artery, biconvex on CT); subdural is slower, venous, elderly/anticoagulated.

questions.stem: A patient with markedly elevated blood pressure presents with facial droop and hemiparesis.
questions.lead: What is the priority in management?
questions.explanation: Nothing else can be decided until you know bleed or clot — CT first. Thrombolysis is contraindicated in haemorrhage and lowering BP is harmful in ischaemia unless very high (>185/110 for lysis).
questions.point: Acute stroke: non-contrast CT before anything else — thrombolysis, BP management and antiplatelets all depend on excluding haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old non-pregnant woman has hypertension refractory to three agents.
questions.lead: Which is the LEAST likely cause?
questions.explanation: Pre-eclampsia is a disease of pregnancy after 20 weeks — irrelevant here. FMD (renal artery stenosis in young women), NF1 (phaeo), renal disease and Conn's are all real secondary causes.
questions.point: Secondary hypertension in a young woman: think renal artery FMD, Conn's, phaeochromocytoma (NF1), renal disease — pre-eclampsia only exists after 20 weeks of pregnancy.

questions.stem: Which is the earliest detectable abnormality in diabetic kidney disease?
questions.lead: What is the earliest routinely screened marker of diabetic kidney disease?
questions.explanation: Moderately increased albuminuria (urine ACR 3–30 mg/mmol, formerly microalbuminuria) precedes any fall in GFR by years, which is why annual ACR screening exists. Strictly the earliest physiological change is glomerular hyperfiltration with a raised GFR, but that is not screened for.
questions.point: Microalbuminuria (urine ACR 3–30 mg/mmol) is the earliest sign of diabetic nephropathy, appearing years before eGFR falls — hence annual ACR screening.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old develops hives within minutes of eating banana yoghurt. He has never previously eaten banana or any cow's milk product.
questions.lead: What is the appropriate next step?
options: Skin-prick testing to identify the allergen
Blood test is required for diagnosis
Diagnose cow's milk allergy and advise avoidance
Diagnose banana allergy and prescribe an adrenaline autoinjector
questions.explanation: Two new foods at once — test before you label. Skin-prick (or specific IgE) directed by the history identifies the culprit; guessing either food risks needless avoidance or a missed real allergy.
questions.point: After a first reaction to a mixed food, identify the allergen with skin-prick or specific IgE testing guided by history before advising avoidance or prescribing adrenaline.

questions.stem: An older man has episodes of severe spinning vertigo lasting under a minute, brought on by rolling over in bed and by looking up. The external ear canal is clear and hearing is normal.
questions.lead: Which would confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Brief positional vertigo is BPPV; Dix–Hallpike provokes the torsional nystagmus and Epley treats it. Tilt table is for orthostatic syncope.
questions.point: Positional vertigo lasting seconds = BPPV: Dix–Hallpike confirms (torsional nystagmus with latency), Epley manoeuvre treats.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old has sudden-onset severe testicular pain and swelling.
questions.lead: What is the appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Sudden testicular pain in a young male is torsion until proven otherwise and the testis has ~6 hours. Do not delay for ultrasound if the clinical suspicion is high.
questions.point: Acute testicular pain in an adolescent/young man = torsion: straight to theatre without waiting for ultrasound — salvage falls sharply after 6 hours.

questions.stem: Which neural circuit is implicated in obsessive-compulsive disorder?
questions.lead: Choose one.
questions.explanation: OCD is a CSTC loop disorder (orbitofrontal–caudate–thalamus). Amygdala circuits are fear/PTSD; mesolimbic is reward/psychosis; nigrostriatal is Parkinson's.
questions.point: OCD is a cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loop disorder; amygdala–hippocampus underlies fear/PTSD and mesolimbic dopamine underlies psychosis and reward.

questions.stem: A woman with osteoporosis has lateral hip pain after bushwalking, worse lying on that side and on resisted abduction, reproduced by point palpation over the greater trochanter. She is weight-bearing and hip X-ray is normal.
questions.lead: What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Point tenderness over the trochanter with lateral pain after activity is gluteal tendinopathy/bursitis. NOF fracture would prevent weight-bearing with a shortened externally rotated leg; OA gives groin pain and restricted internal rotation.
questions.point: Lateral hip pain with point tenderness over the greater trochanter is greater trochanteric pain syndrome; hip OA gives groin pain, and NOF fracture stops weight-bearing.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of vitamin D toxicity?
questions.lead: Choose one.
questions.explanation: Excess vitamin D drives gut absorption of calcium and phosphate — hypercalcaemia with high phosphate and a suppressed PTH. Osteomalacia and raised PTH belong to deficiency.
questions.point: Vitamin D toxicity = hypercalcaemia with raised phosphate and suppressed PTH; deficiency gives low calcium/phosphate, raised PTH and osteomalacia.

questions.stem: A patient has back, arm and leg pain with bony tenderness. Bloods show normochromic normocytic anaemia, hypercalcaemia and a raised creatinine.
questions.lead: What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: CRAB — calcium, renal, anaemia, bone — is myeloma. Paget's has a raised ALP with normal calcium; prostate metastases are sclerotic and rarely hypercalcaemic.
questions.point: Bone pain + hypercalcaemia + renal impairment + normocytic anaemia (CRAB) = multiple myeloma; Paget's has raised ALP with normal calcium.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man has an anterior STEMI (ST elevation V2–V5 with inferior reciprocal depression). The nearest PCI-capable centre is 150 minutes away.
questions.lead: What is the appropriate reperfusion strategy?
options: Aspirin, clopidogrel, enoxaparin and tenecteplase, then transfer
Aspirin, clopidogrel, heparin and transfer for primary PCI
questions.explanation: If primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact, fibrinolysis wins — tenecteplase (bolus, fibrin-specific) with dual antiplatelets and an anticoagulant (enoxaparin or unfractionated heparin), then transfer for angiography. Streptokinase is obsolete in Australia.
questions.point: STEMI with PCI more than 120 minutes from first medical contact: tenecteplase plus aspirin, clopidogrel AND an anticoagulant (enoxaparin/heparin), then transfer for angiography.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old tracking the 50th centile has lost 1 kg in a month. He eats a normal gluten-containing diet, drinks milk, sometimes refuses solids, and has bowel motions that vary between firm and loose.
questions.lead: What is the initial investigation?
questions.explanation: Weight loss with variable stools in a toddler eating gluten warrants coeliac serology first — cheap, non-invasive, and this is the classic presentation age. Real weight loss is never 'normal development'.
questions.point: A toddler losing weight with variable stools on a gluten-containing diet: coeliac serology (anti-tTG IgA with total IgA) is the first investigation.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman with hypertension, heart failure and stage 3 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 42) has an acutely hot, red, exquisitely painful first MTP joint.
questions.lead: What is the appropriate acute treatment?
questions.explanation: Acute gout: NSAIDs are out with CKD and heart failure, so dose-reduced colchicine (or a corticosteroid — oral or intra-articular) is the answer. Allopurinol does not treat a flare. Note the modern nuance: allopurinol no longer has to be deferred — ACR 2020 and the RACGP support starting urate-lowering therapy during a flare provided anti-inflammatory cover is running, because it does not prolong the attack.
questions.point: Acute gout in CKD/heart failure: dose-reduced colchicine or a corticosteroid — NSAIDs contraindicated. Allopurinol does not treat the flare, but starting it during one under anti-inflammatory cover is acceptable and no longer deferred.

questions.stem: An Indigenous man has a rash with raised, serpiginous edges, pain in his hands and knee, and a prolonged PR interval on ECG. He recalls no recent sore throat.
questions.lead: What is the treatment?
questions.explanation: Erythema marginatum, polyarthralgia and a prolonged PR interval in an Indigenous Australian is acute rheumatic fever — and in high-risk populations polyarthralgia counts as a major manifestation, which is how the Jones criteria are met here. The preceding pharyngitis is often unrecalled. Treatment and the first dose of secondary prophylaxis is benzathine benzylpenicillin G IM.
questions.point: Acute rheumatic fever (erythema marginatum, migratory arthritis, prolonged PR) is treated with benzathine penicillin — and long-term secondary prophylaxis — even without a remembered sore throat.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old has had five days of cough with post-tussive vomiting and apnoeic episodes. He received his 6-week immunisations but is not yet due for the 4-month dose. Mother and sister at home also have a cough.
questions.lead: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Paroxysmal cough with post-tussive vomiting and apnoea in an infant with coughing household contacts is pertussis — a single 6-week dose is not protective. Bronchiolitis is wheeze and work of breathing, not paroxysms.
questions.point: Paroxysmal cough with post-tussive vomiting or apnoea in an under-immunised infant with coughing contacts is pertussis; treat with a macrolide and give household prophylaxis.
